one_liner: BLAKE3 in TypeScript with a runtime-generated WASM SIMD module; beats the native napi-rs addon only on inputs under 4 KB.
what_it_does: An npm ESM package (blake3-jit 1.1.0) implementing all three BLAKE3 modes (hash, keyed MAC, derive_key) plus XOF output in pure TypeScript, with no .wasm file to ship: the WebAssembly module is assembled byte by byte in JavaScript and compiled with new WebAssembly.Module on first large hash. API: one-shot hash(input, outputLength?) and zero-allocation hashInto(input, output, outputLength?), plus createHasher/createKeyed/createDeriveKey returning a Hasher with update/finalize/finalizeXof/reset. Input must be a Uint8Array; there is no string, hex or base64 convenience as in @napi-rs/blake-hash.
how_it_is_fast: Below 4 KB (SIMD_THRESHOLD = 4 * CHUNK_LEN in src/hash.ts) it runs a pure-JS compress that applies the Fleek Network blake3js-perf case-study tricks: message and state held in 32 local int32 (SMI) variables with precomputed permutations, module-level reusable typed arrays, and a single Uint32Array view over aligned little-endian input instead of per-block byte assembly; at 96 B to 1 KB this avoids the N-API call and Buffer allocation that dominate the native addon's cost. From 4 KB up, one-shot hash() transposes 4 chunks at a time into WASM linear memory and calls a JIT-emitted compressChunks4x (16 blocks x 4 chunks per call, i32x4 lanes, i8x16.shuffle for the 16- and 8-bit rotations) and a WASM parent-node compress, with the Merkle CV stack kept in a fixed 64 KB arena. That path is only 4 lanes wide and copies every input word through JS typed arrays, which is why native AVX2/AVX-512/NEON code stays ahead on large inputs.
when_to_use: Node.js code hashing many small messages (96 B to 1 KB: cache keys, content IDs, small records) where the author's run shows 1.2x to 2.4x the throughput of the @napi-rs/blake-hash native addon because no FFI crossing happens.
Browsers, Deno, Bun, edge workers or bundles that cannot load native addons or host a separate .wasm asset, and need BLAKE3 from one dependency-free ESM package.
Large one-shot hashes in JS-only environments, where the author reports about 1.36-1.38 GB/s at 32 KB-1 MB (hardware not stated) from the WASM SIMD path.
Code needing keyed MAC, derive_key or XOF in pure JS: the test suite checks all three modes against the official BLAKE3 test vectors (input lengths 0 to 102,400 bytes).
when_not_to_use: Node services hashing buffers of 4 KB and up where a native addon installs: @napi-rs/blake-hash measured 1.97 vs 1.36 GB/s at 32 KB and 2.06 vs 1.38 GB/s at 1 MB in the author's own table (native about 1.5x faster), and the Rust crate's multithreaded mode is not even in the comparison.

Streaming, keyed or derive_key hashing of large data: only one-shot hash()/hashInto() route to WASM SIMD; the Hasher class (update/finalize, createKeyed, createDeriveKey) is pure JS at every size and has no published large-input numbers.

One-shot output longer than 64 bytes: hash()/hashInto() allocate at most a 16-word buffer and throw a RangeError for outputLength above 64; use createHasher().update(x).finalize(n) or finalizeXof() instead.

Pages whose Content Security Policy forbids WebAssembly compilation, or engines without WASM SIMD: initSimdSync() catches the failure, logs console.warn and silently falls back to the pure-JS path for all sizes.
Non-V8 engines when speed matters: docs/optimizations.md lists 'V8 optimizations may not apply to other engines' as a known limitation and no SpiderMonkey or JavaScriptCore numbers are published.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (devDependencies only for tests and benchmarks)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; ESM-only package (type: module); WASM SIMD path needs an engine with fixed-width WebAssembly SIMD (feature-tested with WebAssembly.validate at init), otherwise pure JS
integration.platforms: any JavaScript engine; big-endian hosts and unaligned inputs take a byte-assembly slow path
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded only per the docs: module-level scratch buffers and one shared WASM memory per module instance; each worker thread loads its own instance
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: different function names and return type (Uint8Array, not Buffer), Uint8Array input only (no string, hex/base64 digest or stream helpers), same digests for the default 32-byte output

gotchas: Harness flaw: every size where blake3-jit beats native (96 B, 512 B, 1 KB) runs the pure-JS path, so the win is N-API call and Buffer-allocation overhead, not WebAssembly; the runtime-generated WASM SIMD path (4 KB and up) loses to native at every published size (0.69x at 32 KB, 0.67x at 1 MB, derived from page data).

bench/compare-blake3-fast.ts imports blake3-fast from an untracked ../tmp/blake3-fast build, so the published comparison cannot run from a clean checkout; each row is one 1-second loop after 100 warm-ups with no repeats, CPU or Node version, and the cross-library correctness check uses only a 5-byte input (the SIMD path is covered by the unit tests' official vectors, not by the harness).

README and docs/optimizations.md report different runs (96 B: 362 MB/s in the README, 352 MB/s in the docs, where the comparison column is blake3-fast at 216 MB/s); the README omits the @huggingface/blake3-wasm column the harness also prints.

hash()/hashInto() with outputLength > 64 throw a RangeError (new Uint8Array over a 64-byte buffer); the unit tests exercise one-shot output lengths of only 16, 32 and 64 bytes and never call hashInto().
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over hash-wasm or awasm-noble when you only need BLAKE3, want no .wasm asset at all, and mostly hash inputs under a few KB in Node, where its pure-JS path avoids the boundary crossing; awasm-noble's third-party table (Apple M4) reports a higher 1 MB rate (1,943 MB/s single-threaded, plus a threaded mode), so prefer it for large buffers, and use hash-wasm when you need many algorithms behind one API.
verified_claims_summary: The author's README table compares one-shot hash() against @napi-rs/blake-hash 1.4.0, an N-API addon calling the official blake3 crate's single-threaded blake3::hash (runtime SIMD dispatch, NEON on aarch64), timed in Node with bench/compare-blake3-fast.ts on unstated hardware: 362 vs 149 MB/s at 96 B (2.4x), 748 vs 521 at 512 B, 811 vs 701 at 1 KB, then 1.36 vs 1.97 GB/s at 32 KB and 1.38 vs 2.06 GB/s at 1 MB where native wins.
status_note: Active: renovate commits through 2026-10-07 and release 1.1.0 on 2026-04-17 (npm registry, first release 2025-12-10), MIT, 35 stars, single maintainer (the napi-rs author); Hugging Face published its own fork as @huggingface/blake3-jit and had reset() upstreamed (issue #34).
